chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
title: The first saxophone, a Pan-American, and slipping grades
summary: His father bought a second-hand Pan-American alto in his third year of high school; he played free everywhere, his marks fell, and word spread that he sounded like Hodges.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: I was associated with it. But not for long. Maybe one season or something like that. Because let me see... In my third year in high school, my Daddy decided to buy me a saxophone. Well, I was never a Grade-A student. I would pass, my marks... I was a passable student. But when I got the saxophone, then my marks flopped, because I was out at night playing any place I could for nothing, and running around different places, you know, with my horn under my arm, and get home at 2-3-4-5 in the morning, and then be in school at 8 o'clock in the morning. Well, I'd go to school to sleep. Because you have to sleep sometime!
Do you remember the first horn you had? What make it was?
A Pan-American. A Pan-American horn. Yeah, I remember it. It didn't have any pearl where the
keys are. No pearl. Plain metal.
A silver or a gold color?
No, it was silver. There was no gold in them days.

Are you kiddin'? Brand new?! It was brand new to me, but it was not brand-new. Second-hand horn. Well, I did very good with it, I think. I played around at house parties and one thing or another, and then word got around Boston about some kid around the corner playing saxophone who sounded just like Johnny Hodges. Because you see, Johnny's name was very big. It got very big. And he was known not only all around Boston; all the bands that had come from New York were trying to get him to join their band.
